218.title: Perfume and silver (Mark 14:1–11)
218.hook: a woman anoints him with costly nard; Judas goes to the priests
218.carry: she has done a beautiful thing
218.howItsDone: Christians often read this story at the start of Holy Week; many churches use anointing oil in baptism, confirmation or prayer for the sick, and Christians remember the unnamed woman as an example of extravagant devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a doorkeeper and a single word. Your line was watch. Today the last part of Mark begins: the passion and the empty tomb.

Two days before the Passover. In Jerusalem, the chief priests and scribes want a quiet way to arrest Jesus, but not during the feast, they say, or the people will riot. Out in the village of Bethany, Jesus is at dinner in the house of a man called Simon the leper. A woman comes in carrying an alabaster jar of perfume, pure nard, very expensive. She doesn't dab a little. She breaks the jar and pours the whole thing over his head. The smell fills the house. Every conversation stops. Somebody is already doing the math.
screen: `TWO DAYS BEFORE PASSOVER.` → `AN ALABASTER JAR, BROKEN.` → `SOMEBODY DOES THE MATH.`

segments.voice: Some at the table are indignant. Why this waste? It could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor. And they scold her. Jesus says, in the King James Bible: "Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me." The Greek word for good there, kalos, also means beautiful. She has done a beautiful thing. Then: the poor you always have with you, and you can do them good whenever you want. He's echoing Moses, who said the poor shall never cease out of the land, and so, open your hand to them. In Deuteronomy, that line is a reason to give, not an excuse. Here it's about this moment: you will not always have me. She has done what she could, he says; she has anointed my body beforehand for burying. Remember the word Christ, the anointed one? Here, in Mark, someone anoints him at last, and he says it's for his burial. Wherever the good news is told in the whole world, he promises, what she has done will be told in memory of her. Yet Mark never tells us her name. John's Gospel, telling a similar scene, names her Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus. Then Mark cuts sharply to someone he does name. Judas, one of the twelve, goes to the chief priests to hand him over. They're glad, and promise him money. Perfume poured out for love. Silver taken for a betrayal.

segments.voice: Think of someone you love, and what it would look like to do something extravagant for them: not practical, just beautiful, like a whole afternoon, a letter that takes an hour, or showing up in person when a text would do. Notice the voice that says what a waste, listen to it kindly, and picture doing it anyway. If you pray, offer that love to God too.
Kalos, the Greek word for good, which also means beautiful. A woman pours out costly nard for love, and Judas goes to take silver for a betrayal.
Your line: she has done a beautiful thing. And it's told in memory of her. See you tomorrow.

219.title: The upper room (Mark 14:12–25)
219.hook: take, this is my body; this is my blood of the covenant
219.howItsDone: Christians celebrate this meal as the Eucharist, Mass, Divine Liturgy, Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper, some daily, some weekly, some monthly, repeating Jesus's words over bread and wine; churches differ in how they understand Christ's presence in it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a broken jar of perfume and a bag of silver, kalos. Your line was she has done a beautiful thing.

It's the day the Passover lambs are sacrificed, and the disciples ask: where do you want us to prepare the meal? His instructions sound like a spy novel. Go into the city. You'll meet a man carrying a pitcher of water. Follow him. Wherever he goes in, ask the owner for the guest room, and he'll show you a large upper room, furnished and ready. They find it just as he said. That evening, the twelve recline at the table with him. While they eat, he says it: one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me. They grow sad, and one by one they ask: "Is it I?"
screen: `FOLLOW THE MAN WITH THE WATER JAR.` → `A LARGE UPPER ROOM.` → `IS IT I?`

segments.voice: Nobody points at anyone else. Each one wonders about himself. Then he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them. In the King James Bible: "Take, eat: this is my body." He takes a cup, gives thanks, they all drink from it, and he says: "This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many." That word testament is today's word. In Greek it's diathēkē, and it can mean covenant: a binding agreement. It's why the two halves of the Christian Bible are called the Old and New Testaments, the old and new covenants. At Mount Sinai, Moses sprinkled blood on the people and called it the blood of the covenant. At a Passover meal, the feast of freedom from Egypt, Jesus takes those words onto his own lips. Then he says he won't drink wine again until he drinks it new in the kingdom of God. Christians have gathered around this meal ever since, understanding it in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine truly become his body and blood. Lutherans say he is truly present in, with and under them. Many Reformed Christians speak of a real spiritual presence, and many Baptist and other churches keep it as a memorial. They call it the Eucharist, from the Greek for gave thanks, the Mass, the Divine Liturgy, Holy Communion, the Lord's Supper. And in Mark, over the bread, four verbs: took, blessed, broke, gave.

segments.voice: Hold a piece of bread or a cracker if you have one, or picture the next thing you'll eat, and move slowly through the four verbs: take it, give thanks, break it, share it or eat it, thinking of the people who grew it, baked it, carried it. This isn't communion, just a meal eaten with thanks. If you pray, you can give thanks to God before you eat.
Covenant. In Greek, diathēkē: a binding promise, and the old English word testament. The new covenant, in a cup.
Your line: take, this is my body. Bread broken, and given. Day two hundred nineteen.

220.title: Even if all fall away (Mark 14:26–31)
220.hook: after a hymn, Peter swears he'll never desert him
220.howItsDone: Many Christians remember Peter's boast and later failure in Holy Week services, and they often point to him as a sign that God keeps faith with people who overestimate their own strength.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was covenant, a binding promise, in bread and cup in the upper room. Your line was take, this is my body.

The meal is over. Mark gives it one quiet line, in the King James Bible: "And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives." A Passover meal traditionally closed with the psalms of praise called the Hallel, and those end with Psalm 118: the stone the builders rejected, blessed is he that cometh. So they walk out singing, into the dark, across the valley, up the hill. On the way, Jesus says something that stops them. Tonight, all of you will fall away because of me. It is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. Silence on the path. Then one voice, the one you'd expect, speaks up at once.
screen: `THEY SANG A HYMN.` → `OUT INTO THE DARK.` → `ALL OF YOU WILL FALL AWAY.`

segments.voice: Peter says: "Although all shall be offended, yet will not I." Even if everyone else falls away, not me. And he means it. He loves Jesus, and he believes he's strong enough. Jesus answers with painful precision: "this day, even in this night, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice." Only Mark has the rooster crow twice. Peter doubles down, louder: "If I should die with thee, I will not deny thee in any wise." Then Mark adds five small, devastating words: "Likewise also said they all." The word the King James translates offended is skandalizō in Greek. It comes from a skandalon, the trigger stick of a trap, the thing that trips you. It's where English gets the word scandal. So falling away isn't a slow drift. It's getting caught, suddenly, by something you didn't see. And here's the part almost everyone skips. Between the warning and Peter's boast, Jesus slips in a promise: "But after that I am risen, I will go before you into Galilee." Before they've failed, he's already arranged to meet them afterward. The shepherd will be struck, the sheep will scatter, and the shepherd will go ahead of them to gather them again. Christians have found great comfort in that order: the failure foreseen, the meeting planned first. Peter's courage is real, and it isn't enough. What holds is not his promise to Jesus, but Jesus's promise to him.
screen: `YET WILL NOT I.` · `THE COCK WILL CROW TWICE.` · `SKANDALON: THE TRIGGER OF A TRAP.` · `I WILL GO BEFORE YOU INTO GALILEE.` · then, large: `LIKEWISE ALSO SAID THEY ALL.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've promised, to yourself or someone else, with total confidence: I'll never snap at the kids again, I'll definitely stay calm, I'd never do that. Hold it gently, and instead of doubling down, try saying: I want to, and I may not manage it; notice whether that feels weaker, or truer. If you pray, ask for help rather than promising strength.
Skandalon, the trigger stick of a trap, a stumbling block. Peter's promise: not me. Sincere, and not strong enough.
Your line: not I, said Peter. But Galilee was planned first. That's day two hundred twenty.

221.title: Abba (Mark 14:32–42)
221.hook: in Gethsemane he calls God Abba, Father, and asks for the cup to pass
221.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Jesus's words "not what I will, but what thou wilt" in times of struggle, and some churches keep a watch of prayer late on Maundy Thursday night in memory of Gethsemane.

segments.voice: Yesterday, skandalon: Peter said, not me. Your line was not I said Peter.

After supper they go out to the Mount of Olives, to a place called Gethsemane. Tradition says the name means oil press, the place where olives are crushed. Jesus tells most of the disciples to sit and wait, and takes Peter, James and John a little further. Then Mark says something about Jesus you haven't heard before: he began to be deeply distressed and troubled. He tells them, in the King James Bible: "My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death: tarry ye here, and watch." He goes a little further on alone, and falls on the ground. Not kneeling, composed. On the ground. And the first word out of his mouth is today's word.
screen: `A PLACE CALLED GETHSEMANE.` → `SORROWFUL UNTO DEATH.` → `FACE DOWN ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: "Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt." Abba is an Aramaic word. Mark keeps it, then translates it for his Greek readers: Father. You may have heard that abba means daddy. Mark doesn't say that; he gives it simply as Father. And Paul, writing in Greek to grown men and women, keeps the word too: they cry Abba, Father. So whatever else it is, it isn't baby talk. It's family talk, said by a son in the dark. Listen to the whole prayer. All things are possible to you: the same words he gave the father of the boy, and the disciples at the needle's eye. Take away this cup: Isaiah speaks of a cup of trembling. Then the turn: not what I will, but what you will. He asks honestly for what he wants, then hands it over. He comes back, and they're asleep. "Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?" Watch, the word from a few days ago. "The spirit truly is ready, but the flesh is weak." He goes and prays the same words again. Comes back: asleep. A third time. Then: it is enough. The hour has come. Rise up, let's go. Many Christians see here both how human Jesus was and how he trusted. In the dark, face down, he still says Abba.
screen: `ABBA: MARK SAYS FATHER.` · `NOT DADDY, BUT NOT DISTANT.` · `TAKE THIS CUP, YET THY WILL.` · `COULDEST NOT THOU WATCH ONE HOUR?` · then, large: `NOT WHAT I WILL, BUT WHAT THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: Think of what you'd say if you could be completely honest with someone who loves you: what do you want taken away, and what are you afraid of? If you pray, speak to God the way Jesus did, Abba, Father, say plainly what you want, and then, only if you can, add his next words: nevertheless, not what I will, but what thou wilt. If you don't pray, just let yourself be honest, like a child would be.
Abba. Aramaic for father, the word a child uses at home. Jesus's first word in Gethsemane.
Your line: abba, father. Honest words, said face down in the dark at Gethsemane. Until tomorrow.

222.title: The kiss and the linen (Mark 14:43–52)
222.hook: betrayed with a kiss; a young man flees naked, a detail only Mark keeps
222.howItsDone: Christians remember the arrest on Maundy Thursday night and Good Friday, and some churches strip the altar bare in silence after the Thursday service as a sign of Jesus left alone.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Abba, prayed face down in Gethsemane. Your line was abba, father.

He's still speaking to his sleepy friends when Judas arrives, one of the twelve, with a crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. Judas has given them a signal, so they take the right man. In the King James Bible: "Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he; take him, and lead him away safely." Judas walks straight up to Jesus, says, "Master, master," and kisses him. When he plans the signal, Mark's Greek uses the plain word for kiss. When he does it, Mark uses a longer form, and some readers hear it as warm, the way you'd greet someone you love.
screen: `A CROWD WITH SWORDS AND CLUBS.` → `THE SIGNAL IS A KISS.` → `MASTER, MASTER.`

segments.voice: They seize him. Someone standing by pulls a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant. Mark doesn't say who; John's Gospel later names Peter. Jesus speaks to the crowd: have you come out with swords and clubs as if I were a bandit? Day after day I was with you in the temple, teaching, and you didn't arrest me. But let the scriptures be fulfilled. Then the sentence the whole evening has been leading to: "And they all forsook him, and fled." Earlier that night they all said they'd die with him. Now every one is running through the dark. Then something strange, which Matthew and Luke leave out. "And there followed him a certain young man, having a linen cloth cast about his naked body." They grab him, and he wriggles out of the cloth and runs off naked, leaving them holding the linen. Who was he? The text is silent. An old guess says it was Mark himself, signing his gospel with an embarrassing memory. Some readers hear an echo of the prophet Amos: on that day even the bravest will flee away naked. Others notice the linen, because a linen cloth will appear again later in this story, and so will a young man. The picture is clear: one last follower, trying to stay close, leaves everything and runs. Christians have often seen themselves here. Not in the kiss, but in the running. And they notice that the one left alone is the one who does not run.

segments.voice: People flee hard things in different ways: some go silent, some go busy, some scroll, some make a joke, some leave the room. Without scolding yourself, notice yours the way you'd notice a habit in a friend, and picture the last time you ran and what you left behind in someone else's hands. If you pray, you can bring that moment to God honestly.
Amos, the prophet some readers hear echoed here: on that day even the bravest will flee away naked.
Your line: they all fled. And he did not run. Day two hundred twenty-two, done.

223.title: I am (Mark 14:53–65)
223.hook: before the high priest, silent until asked: are you the Christ? I am
223.howItsDone: Christians read Jesus's trial before the council in Holy Week, and many churches read the whole passion story aloud on Palm Sunday or Good Friday, often with different readers taking the parts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a kiss in the dark garden, Amos, and your line was they all fled.

The same night. They lead Jesus from the garden to the high priest, and the chief priests, elders and scribes gather there. Outside in the courtyard, Peter has followed at a distance and is warming his hands at a fire. Hold on to him; he's tomorrow. Inside, the council is looking for testimony that will stick. Witness after witness stands up, and their stories don't match. Some say they heard Jesus threaten to destroy the temple and build another in three days. Even on that, Mark says, they don't agree. Through all of it, the man on trial says nothing.
screen: `THE HIGH PRIEST'S HOUSE, AT NIGHT.` → `WITNESSES WHO DON'T AGREE.` → `HE SAYS NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Finally the high priest stands up in the middle of the room. Aren't you going to answer? What is it these men testify against you? Silence. In the King James Bible: "But he held his peace, and answered nothing." Accused, it's easy to start talking fast: explaining, correcting, defending. He doesn't. The false stories fall apart on their own. Then the high priest asks the one question that matters: "Art thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? And Jesus said, I am." The Son of the Blessed is a respectful way of saying God without saying the name. And notice the change. Again and again in Mark, Jesus has told people to keep quiet about who he is. Now, on trial, with everything to lose, he answers plainly. The silence and the answer come from the same place: he isn't reacting to pressure; he knows what is worth saying. In Greek, I am is two words, ego eimi: ordinary Greek, the way anyone would say it's me. Some readers also hear an echo of the burning bush, where God tells Moses his name is I am that I am. Readers differ on how much Mark means that here. Then Jesus adds a line from Daniel and the Psalms: they will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of power, coming with the clouds of heaven. The high priest tears his clothes, the council calls it blasphemy and condemns him, and some begin to spit and strike him, and mock him: prophesy!

segments.voice: Picture a moment where you might feel accused, rushed or judged, a meeting, a text thread, a family dinner, and picture not rushing to defend yourself: just a breath, then another, noticing the urge to explain in your chest and jaw without obeying it. Then ask: if I speak, what is the one true thing worth saying? If you pray, hold that moment before God in the quiet.
I am. Two plain words, ego eimi in Greek, spoken after a long silence, when the high priest asks if he is the Christ.
Your line: silence can be strong. And two plain words can be enough. Day two hundred twenty-three.

224.title: Peter by the fire (Mark 14:66–72)
224.hook: a servant girl, a denial, the rooster twice, and Peter breaks down weeping
224.howItsDone: Christians read Peter's denial in Holy Week, and a rooster became a common symbol of Peter and of repentance, carved on church towers and pictured in art of his weeping.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a trial at night and two words, I am. Your line was silence can be strong.

While Jesus stands before the council upstairs, Mark cuts back to the courtyard below. Peter is there, the one who said earlier that same night, even if everyone else falls away, not I. When the others fled, he followed, at a distance, right into the high priest's courtyard. That took courage. He's sitting with the servants by a fire, warming himself. One of the high priest's servant girls walks past, stops, and really looks at him. You were with the Nazarene, she says. You were with Jesus. Not a soldier, not a judge: a young woman with a job to do, and one sentence.
screen: `MEANWHILE, THE COURTYARD.` → `A FIRE, AND PETER.` → `YOU WERE WITH JESUS.`

segments.voice: I don't know what you're talking about, Peter says, and he moves out to the gateway. A rooster crows. The girl sees him again and tells the people standing around: this is one of them. He denies it again. A little later the bystanders try: surely you're one of them, you're a Galilean; they can hear it in his accent. And Peter, in the King James Bible, "began to curse and to swear, saying, I know not this man of whom ye speak." Three denials, each one louder. Right then the rooster crows a second time, just as Jesus said: before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice. Then Mark gives one short, plain sentence: "And when he thought thereon, he wept." The Greek behind when he thought thereon is rare and hard to pin down. Translators have guessed: he broke down, he threw himself down, he covered his head. Nobody is sure. But the verb for wept is clear, and its tense suggests he kept on weeping. Notice the timing. Upstairs, Jesus tells the truth, and it will cost him his life. Downstairs, Peter lies to save his. Mark sets them side by side. Tradition links Mark's gospel to Peter's own preaching; if so, Peter told this story on himself. He doesn't hide the failure. The weeping is where he starts again. This week went from perfume, to the upper room, to a garden where he prayed abba, to a kiss, a trial, and now a fire.

Sadness isn't the end of the story: for Peter, it was the turning point. If you pray, you can bring that failure to God as it is.
Peter, warming himself by the fire while three denials slip out, and a rooster crows twice. Then he breaks down weeping.
Your line: he wept. And the story didn't stop there. Day two hundred twenty-four closes the week.
